summary: Describes TAMP, a transport-independent protocol for managing trust anchors and community identifiers in a trust anchor store. It uses the Cryptographic Message Syntax and digital signatures for integrity and origin authentication. It is a Proposed Standard.

eli5.summary: A list of trusted friends needs updating when someone moves. This is a signed message system for adding and removing them safely.

questions: what is an apex trust anchor
subtitle: How a device's list of trusted signing keys is queried, updated and replaced safely, using signed CMS messages.

tldr.problem: Devices such as cryptographic modules rely on trust anchors, public keys they trust to validate signatures, and those keys sometimes must be added, removed or replaced after the device is deployed.
tldr.mechanism: TAMP defines eleven Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) message types for querying and updating a trust anchor store. Update requests are signed, and sequence numbers detect replay.
tldr.outcome: A trust anchor manager can change a store's trust anchors and community identifiers, and can even replace the top-level apex trust anchor, over any transport. Confidentiality is not provided.

today: RFC 5934 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the trust anchor formats in RFC 5914.

sections.title: What TAMP Does
sections.content:
The Trust Anchor Management Protocol (TAMP) manages the trust anchors and community identifiers in any device that uses digital signatures. The RFC says it was written with the needs of cryptographic modules in mind. For example, a trust anchor public key can validate signatures on signed firmware packages (RFC 4108).

Most TAMP messages are digitally signed for integrity and data origin authentication. Signed and unsigned messages both use the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 5652). The protocol is transport independent: messages may be exchanged in real time, or stored and moved by other means. An exchange is a request plus, optionally, a response. A GPS receiver, for instance, might show the result on an attached display instead of sending a reply.

TAMP does not provide confidentiality. If it is required, the communications environment must supply it.
sections.eli5: TAMP is a way to send signed instructions to a device saying which keys it should trust. The device may answer, or may just show a message on its screen.

sections.title: Trust Anchors and Their Three Roles
sections.content:
A trust anchor holds a public key used to validate digital signatures, plus a public key identifier. TAMP accepts three formats: Certificate and TBSCertificate (RFC 5280) and TrustAnchorInfo (RFC 5914), a minimalist form for constrained storage or bandwidth. A key can validate a signature directly, or validate an X.509 certification path whose final certificate's key checks the signature. Implementations MUST support the direct case; the path case is OPTIONAL.

By function there are three types:

  • Apex trust anchor: exactly one per store, superior to all others and unconstrained. It may hold an operational public key and a contingency public key.
  • Management trust anchors: used to manage the module, for example to validate TAMP messages and signed firmware.
  • Identity trust anchors: used to validate certification paths for non-management applications.

The contingency key can only be used to sign an Apex Trust Anchor Update that replaces both keys. It is stored encrypted, and the decryption key arrives inside the very message it validates.
sections.eli5: The store has one boss key, some manager keys and some everyday keys. The boss also has a sealed spare key that is only unsealed in an emergency, to hand the job to a new boss.

sections.title: Required Building Blocks
sections.content:
TAMP does not assume a particular architecture but REQUIRES four elements: a cryptographic module, a trust anchor store, TAMP protocol processing and other application-specific protocol processing.

Each trust anchor store MUST have a unique name and SHOULD be able to hold one or more community identifiers, which are object identifiers naming a collection of modules that can be the target of one message. If apex support is provided, the store MUST hold exactly one apex trust anchor. Each trust anchor MUST have a unique public key, and a key MUST NOT appear twice in a store. The store MUST also keep a sequence number for each trust anchor allowed to generate TAMP messages.

The cryptographic module MUST support at least one hash function, one signature validation algorithm and one signature generation algorithm. As with RFC 5280, TAMP does not mandate particular algorithms.
sections.eli5: To work, the device needs a safe place to keep its trusted keys, a signature checker, and a unique name so messages can be aimed at it.

sections.title: The CMS Wrapper and Message Types
sections.content:
Signed TAMP messages are a CMS ContentInfo holding SignedData (id-signedData, 1.2.840.113549.1.7.2). Its version MUST be 3, it has a single digest algorithm and exactly one SignerInfo, and signedAttrs is REQUIRED. The signed attributes MUST include content-type and message-digest and MAY include binary-signing-time. The content type names which TAMP message is inside. Unsigned messages place the message directly in ContentInfo.

Everything is encoded with DER (the single-form subset of BER) so that signatures are well defined. DER is REQUIRED for all TAMP structures, signed or not. Unrecognized signed attributes MUST be ignored. The one normal use of an unsigned attribute is the contingency-public-key-decrypt-key in an Apex Trust Anchor Update validated by the contingency key.

TAMP specifies eleven message types. Trust anchor managers send the queries and updates. Trust anchor stores send the responses, confirms and errors. Query, update, community update and sequence adjust messages MUST be signed. Responses SHOULD be signed, and MUST be if the implementation can sign. Support for Trust Anchor Update is REQUIRED; the rest is RECOMMENDED. Queries and updates ask for either a terse or a verbose response.
sections.eli5: Every message goes in a standard envelope with a label saying what kind it is and the sender's signature. The envelope is always packed the same way so the signature can be checked exactly.

sections.title: Querying and Updating a Store
sections.content:
A Status Query asks which trust anchors and communities a store has. A valid one SHOULD get a Status Response, otherwise a TAMP Error SHOULD be returned. Messages name their targets with a TargetIdentifier: hardware module types and serial numbers (singly or as a block), communities, allModules, a URI, or an otherName. Implementations MUST support allModules.

A Trust Anchor Update adds, removes or changes management and identity trust anchors. It cannot touch the apex trust anchor. The updates are processed in order and independently, so a failure does not stop the rest. Adding an anchor that is already identical, or removing one that is absent, counts as success. Changing a missing anchor fails with trustAnchorNotFound, and a change using the wrong structure type fails with improperTAChange. The store returns a Trust Anchor Update Confirm with one status code per update.

An Apex Trust Anchor Update replaces the apex key or keys. It must be validated directly by the operational or contingency key, with no certification path. It can also set clearTrustAnchors and clearCommunities to wipe the other anchors and community identifiers.

A Community Update adds or removes community identifiers. The whole batch must succeed or the list is left unchanged, and removals are done before additions. A Sequence Number Adjust resets the signer's stored sequence number. The TAMP Error message reports why an invalid request failed.
sections.eli5: The manager can ask the device what it trusts, add or remove trusted names, change the boss key, edit the club lists, or fix the message counter. Each request gets a signed reply saying what happened.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Subordination
sections.content:
Sequence numbers give replay protection. Each originator MUST treat its number as a monotonically increasing non-negative integer. For messages validated directly by a trust anchor, the store MUST check that the number is greater than the last successfully processed one from that signer, otherwise it MUST reject with seqNumFailure. Sequence Number Adjust is the exception: an equal value is accepted. Numbers are 64-bit non-negative integers, allowing 9,223,372,036,854,775,807 messages before the signer MUST move to a new key pair. A newly authorized signer starts at zero and its first message is not rejected by the check.

Subordination checks stop a signer from granting more authority than it has. For each individual update, the signer's constraints MUST be greater than or equal to those of the anchor in the update. Policy flags may only be set false if the signer's are false. Certificate policies are intersected, excluded names are unioned, and permitted names are intersected. The new anchor's name must lie inside the signer's permitted names and outside its excluded names. The apex trust anchor is unconstrained, so updates it signs skip these checks.
sections.eli5: Each note carries a counter that must always go up, so an old copy of a note is turned away. A helper can never hand out more power than the helper has.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because state-changing messages are signed, no further integrity or origin authentication is needed, but no confidentiality is offered either. The RFC treats trust anchor configurations and manager certificates as not sensitive.

The RFC walks through key compromise. A stolen identity anchor key lets an attacker issue certificates accepted by every store with that anchor, within its path controls. A stolen management key lets the attacker configure all devices holding it within the subordination limits, and if it also governs firmware, install different firmware. Compromise of the apex operational key lets the attacker configure the devices as desired and sign messages of any content type. The optional contingency key is the recovery route.

Other points: name comparison in certification paths is complex, so any certificate profile SHOULD use simple names and avoid case conversion and whitespace handling. Weak random number generators undermine signatures. TrustAnchorList input has no replay detection. Managers that lose sequence-number state risk seqNumFailure and can recover it from logged messages or with a Status Query.
sections.eli5: If a thief steals a key, the thief can do whatever that key was allowed to do. The boss key is the most dangerous to lose, which is why a sealed spare exists.

viz.caption: THE THREE TYPES OF TRUST ANCHOR

items.title: Apex
items.text: One per store, unconstrained, can hold operational and contingency keys.

items.title: Management
items.text: Validates TAMP messages and other management content such as signed firmware.

items.title: Identity
items.text: Anchors certification paths for non-management applications.
